title: Virtuoso: Enabling Fast and Accurate Virtual Memory Research via an Imitation-based Operating System Simulation Methodology
problem: Existing virtual memory (VM) simulation tools either lack accuracy in modeling OS software components (e.g., page table walks, TLB shootdowns, OS scheduling interactions) or are too slow and complex to prototype hardware/OS co-designs spanning the hardware/software boundary.
motivation: Virtual memory has become a major performance bottleneck due to surging data demands from emerging applications, and the complexity of hardware/OS co-design evaluation is impeding research progress.
method: Virtuoso uses a lightweight simulator that learns from real operating system behavior. It records the decisions an OS makes about managing virtual memory—allocating memory pages, freeing unused ones, and managing the TLB (a hardware cache that stores address translations). The simulator learns to copy these patterns, then replays them with accurate timing measurements when testing new hardware or OS designs. This runs much faster than simulating the entire operating system.
key_novelty: A simulator learns from real OS behavior to quickly reproduce virtual memory decisions in new hardware and software designs, avoiding the need for full operating system simulation.
contributions: Identification of accuracy and speed limitations in current VM simulation methodologies
Imitation-based OS simulation methodology that captures and replays OS virtual memory decisions
Fast and accurate simulation framework enabling hardware/OS co-design evaluation across diverse workloads and systems
baselines: existing VM simulation tools (unnamed in abstract)
limitations: Imitation fidelity depends on quality and coverage of OS training traces; behavior on unseen workloads or OS configurations not discussed.
primary_theme: imitation-based OS simulation for virtual memory research
